findings.summary: acquireExclusive phase 2 never heartbeats the exclusive marker. take() writes heartbeatAt once; the holder then waits up to maxWaitMs (60 min default) for running slot holders with no further heartbeat (the first comes only from runAll). Failure scenario: a full-scope verify takes the marker while an affected verify holds slot-0 and runs more than 25 min in total (likely: several commands of up to 20 min each). The marker is then reported 'stale', so every new acquirer waiting on it is refused at once with 'blocked by a stale holder ... Stop that process'. Machine verifies run unslotted next to the full suite, defeating AISDLC-1378, and pre-push refuses the push, all while the holder is healthy. Fix: call slot.heartbeat() each phase-2 iteration before await wait(...). Add a test where phase 2 outlasts VERIFY_SLOT_STALE_MS and a second caller is told to wait, not refused.

findings.summary: The pre-push holder heartbeats only once per package, and its test:coverage run has no 20-minute per-command timeout, which VERIFY_SLOT_STALE_MS (25 min) relies on. A slow coverage run on a loaded machine would be reported stale and trigger fail-fast refusals for other waiters. Consider a heartbeat interval during the run, or documenting the assumption.

findings.summary: processStartTime() runs `ps -o lstart= -p <pid>` through execFileSync. It passes no shell, the argv is fixed and the pid comes from String(number), so command injection is not possible. The pre-push coverage hook (scripts/pre-push-patch-coverage.mjs) now reaches this call through acquireVerifySlot, so a process started from a git hook inherits `{ ...process.env, LC_ALL: 'C' }`, including any GIT_DIR / GIT_WORK_TREE / GIT_INDEX_FILE / GIT_PREFIX. `ps` never reads those variables and runs no git command, so I see no way to exploit this and it is not a parent-checkout risk. The AISDLC-1129 rule still asks the change to say how it handles them. A one-line comment saying they are kept on purpose because `ps` ignores them, or a scrub with gitSafeEnv(), would close the declaration gap.

findings.summary: The stale-holder refusal tells the operator to 'Stop that process or remove its directory'. That is consistent with acceptance criterion 4: the code itself never kills or reclaims a live holder. holder.json is read with JSON.parse and every field is type-checked, and the file sits on the same user's local board directory, so it is not a new trust boundary. Any local process running as the same user could forge holder.json to make a slot look stale or reused. That is the same same-user trust model already documented for the board, so I am not raising it as a vulnerability.

findings.summary: The exclusive phase-1 loop has no bound and no await in one case. `take()` swallows every mkdir error. If mkdir fails for a reason other than EEXIST, the marker directory does not exist. That happens when `verify-slots/` is removed after the earlier recursive mkdir, or when it is not writable. Then `inspect()` returns null, `blocks(null)` is false and `wait()` is never called. The loop spins synchronously, so the event loop never runs again and the maxWaitMs bound never applies. The old code at least slept on each pass. This works against the 'no caller waits forever' requirement. Fix: when take() fails and the holder does not block, still call `wait('the exclusive full-scope marker', [], 'any')` or throw after a retry, so the time limit applies.
